\title{Metric Markov cotype two of $\ell_1$ with $C^2=3024$: a machine-checked proof}
\date{}
\begin{document}
\maketitle
\begin{abstract}
We present a Lean 4 / Mathlib formalization of the statement that the real space $\ell_1$ has metric Markov cotype two with constant $C^2=3024$, that is, $N_2(\ell_1)\le 12\sqrt{21}$. For every reversible stochastic matrix $A$ on $n\ge1$ states with probability vector $\pi$, every $t\ge1$ and all $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\ell_1$, there are $y_1,\dots,y_n\in\ell_1$ with $\sum_i\pi_i\|x_i-y_i\|_1^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_ia_{ij}\|y_i-y_j\|_1^2\le 3024\sum_{i,j}\pi_i(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s)_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_1^2$. The formal proof follows the source argument: cut decomposition, the cubic map $3r^2-2r^3$ with a quartic potential, a resolvent-harmonic extension, and a comparison of geometric and Ces\`aro averages. The martingale and the random geometric time are replaced by deterministic sums against the resolvent matrix. The whole proof is checked by Lean; the constant is $108\cdot 28=3024$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Statement}

Let $\ell_1$ be the real Banach space of real sequences $x=(x(k))_{k}$ with $\norm{x}_1=\sum_k\abs{x(k)}<\infty$. Write $[n]$ for an $n$-element index set.

A matrix $A=(a_{ij})_{i,j\in[n]}$ is \emph{stochastic} if its entries are nonnegative and every row sums to $1$. A \emph{probability vector} $\pi=(\pi_i)_{i\in[n]}$ has nonnegative entries summing to $1$; zero entries are allowed. $A$ is \emph{reversible} with respect to $\pi$ if $\pi_ia_{ij}=\pi_ja_{ji}$ for all $i,j$. $A^s$ denotes the $s$-th matrix power.

\begin{theorem}[metric Markov cotype two of $\ell_1$, $C^2=3024$]
Let $n,t\ge 1$ be integers, $\pi$ a probability vector on $[n]$, $A$ a stochastic matrix on $[n]$ reversible with respect to $\pi$, and $x_1,\dots,x_n\in\ell_1$. Then there exist $y_1,\dots,y_n\in\ell_1$ with
\[
 \sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}_1^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_ia_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}_1^2
 \le 3024\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tA^s\Bigr)_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}_1^2 .
\]
\end{theorem}

The source proof uses reversibility only through stationarity, $\pi A=\pi$.

\section{Formalization}

The formalization uses Mathlib. It relies on Mathlib's space $\ell^p$ (the type \texttt{lp}), its finite and infinite sums, and its matrix powers. No other earlier results are used.

\paragraph{Index sets.} The index set $[n]$ is Lean's $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$. $\Pow([n])$ denotes the set of \emph{all} subsets of $[n]$, including $\emptyset$ and $[n]$. For $B\in\Pow([n])$ and $i\in[n]$ put $\one_B(i)=1$ if $i\in B$ and $0$ otherwise. We write $\delta_{ij}$ for the entries of the identity matrix.

\paragraph{Infinite sums.} We say that a series $\sum_s f(s)$ of reals \emph{converges to $a$} if it converges unconditionally (Mathlib's \texttt{HasSum}). For real series this is equivalent to absolute convergence with sum $a$. When a hypothesis contains $\sum_{s=0}^\infty f(s)$, this is Mathlib's \texttt{tsum}. It equals the sum when $f$ is summable and is $0$ otherwise. Every such series below is shown to be summable (\cref{lem:res_summable}).

\paragraph{The space $\ell_1$.} The space is Mathlib's $\ell^1$ of real sequences indexed by $\N=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$. Its elements are sequences $x$ with $\sum_k\abs{x(k)}<\infty$, with coordinatewise operations and norm $\norm{x}=\sum_{k\ge0}\abs{x(k)}$. Shifting the index from $\{1,2,\dots\}$ to $\{0,1,\dots\}$ is an isometric relabeling.

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{setting_stationary}]\label{lem:setting_stationary}
Let $\pi:[n]\to\R$ be arbitrary and let $A$ be stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$. Then $\sum_i\pi_iA_{ij}=\pi_j$ for every $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $s$. The case $s=0$ is $\sum_i\pi_i\delta_{ij}=\pi_j$.

For the step, write $A^{s+1}=A^sA$. Exchanging sums gives
\[
\sum_i\pi_i(A^{s+1})_{ij}=\sum_l\Bigl(\sum_i\pi_i(A^s)_{il}\Bigr)A_{lj}=\sum_l\pi_lA_{lj}.
\]
The last expression equals $\pi_j$ by the argument of \cref{lem:setting_stationary}.
\end{proof}

The target asserts the following; this is also the statement proved by \leanname{solution} in the last subsection. Let $n,t$ be natural numbers with $0<n$ and $0<t$. Let $\pi:[n]\to\R$ be a probability vector, $A$ a stochastic matrix reversible with respect to $\pi$, and $x:[n]\to\ell_1$. Then there exists $y:[n]\to\ell_1$ with
\[
 \sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+t\sum_i\sum_j\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2
 \le 3024\sum_i\sum_j\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
This is exactly the source theorem:
\begin{itemize}
\item The hypotheses $0<n$ and $0<t$ encode $n,t\in\{1,2,\dots\}$.
\item $\norm{\cdot}$ is the $\ell_1$ norm.
\item The entry of the Ces\`aro average is written as $\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t(A^s)_{ij}$.
\end{itemize}
Reversibility is kept as a hypothesis, as in the source. The proof uses it only through \cref{lem:setting_stationary_pow}. The more general statement for stationary matrices (the source's closing remark) is not formalized.

\section{Proof}

\subsection{Overview}

Throughout, $q=t/(t+1)$ and $p=1-q=1/(t+1)$, as in the source. The \emph{resolvent matrix} is
\[
G_{ij}=\sum_{s\ge0}(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}.
\]
In probabilistic terms, $G_{ij}=\mathbb P_i(X_S=j)$ for the geometric time $S$ of the source.

\paragraph{Cut decomposition (source Lemma 1).}
\begin{itemize}
\item \cref{lem:cut_coord_upper_reduce,lem:cut_coord_upper_shift,lem:cut_coord_upper,lem:cut_coord_core,lem:cut_coord} treat one real coordinate. They decompose $a:[n]\to\R$ into nested upper cuts.
\item \cref{lem:cut_l1_ext,lem:cut_l1_apply,lem:cut_l1_norm_combo,lem:cut_l1_vectors_summable_fsum,lem:cut_l1_vectors,lem:cut_l1} assemble the coordinates into vectors $\beta_B\in\ell_1$. They produce the binary codes $z_i$, the weights $w_B=\norm{\beta_B}$ and the $1$-Lipschitz affine map $T$.
\end{itemize}
Deviations from the source:
\begin{itemize}
\item The cut vectors are built by induction on the number of distinct values, not by the explicit formula $(\min_B-\max_{B^c})_+$.
\item All subsets $B\in\Pow([n])$ are kept, with weights $w_B\ge0$ that may vanish, so there is no separate ``all points coincide'' case.
\item The base point of $T$ is $x_{i_0}$ for the first index $i_0$, rather than the coordinatewise minimum. This is why $n>0$ is needed.
\item The identity $\norm{x_i-x_j}_1=\norm{z_i-z_j}_H^2$ is not stated separately. It is used in \cref{lem:assembly_real} through $(z_{iB}-z_{kB})^2=\abs{z_{kB}-z_{iB}}$ for bits.
\item No Hilbert space is introduced. All quantities are explicit weighted sums.
\end{itemize}

\paragraph{The flat map (source Lemma 2).} \cref{lem:flat_scalar,lem:flat_increment,lem:flat_ineq}, with $\phi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$. The scalar estimate is proved algebraically from
\[
\phi(r')-\phi(r)=\delta\bigl(6r(1-r)+\delta(3-4r-2r')\bigr),\qquad \delta=r'-r,
\]
instead of by integration.

\paragraph{Martingale step (source Corollary 3 and Section 4.1).} There is no probability space, martingale or filtration. Instead:
\begin{itemize}
\item \cref{lem:local_ineq_combine,lem:local_ineq} state the one-step inequality for a convex combination. The balance relation $u=pv+\sum_jc_jU_j$ plays the role of the martingale property, and the linear terms cancel exactly.
\item \cref{lem:global_sum} sums these one-step inequalities with weights $\pi_kG_{ki}$, where $k$ is the starting state (the centre $e=z_k$) and $i$ the current live state. It telescopes the quartic potential with the identity $G=pI+qGA$ (\cref{lem:res_right}) and stationarity $\pi G=\pi$ (\cref{lem:res_stationary}). This is the source's computation of $\mathbb E\sum_m$ along the killed chain, multiplied by $p$.
\item The source's exact identity $B+tE_A$ is replaced by the decomposition of \cref{lem:assembly_real_split} and the division by $p$ in \cref{lem:assembly_real_finish}.
\end{itemize}
The resolvent facts are \cref{lem:res_summable,lem:res_nonneg,lem:res_rowsum,lem:res_stationary_hasSum_fin,lem:res_stationary,lem:res_left,lem:res_right}. The harmonic extension $h=Gz$ is \cref{lem:h_props}. The assembly is \cref{lem:assembly_real,lem:assembly}.

\paragraph{Comparison of costs (source Lemma 4).} The random time $S$ is replaced by the geometric weights $(1-q)q^s$, and $J,R$ by $\lfloor s/t\rfloor$ and $s\bmod t$:
\begin{itemize}
\item subadditivity of $\sqrt{D}$: \cref{lem:stoch_pow,lem:weighted_minkowski,lem:markov_subadd_expand,lem:markov_subadd_left,lem:markov_subadd_right,lem:markov_subadd};
\item the bounds $D(t)\le4W$ and the block estimate: \cref{lem:comp_Dt,lem:comp_block};
\item the geometric moments: \cref{lem:comp_geom_sq_sqsum,lem:comp_geom_sq,lem:comp_geom_mod_pow_le,lem:comp_geom_mod_hasSum,lem:comp_geom_mod};
\item the conclusion: \cref{lem:comp_real_range,lem:comp_real,lem:res_comparison}.
\end{itemize}
The bound $\mathbb P(R=r)\le 2/t$ becomes the closed form for $\sum_sq^sf(s\bmod t)$.

\paragraph{Hypotheses actually used.} Only $\pi_i\ge0$ is used; the normalization $\sum_i\pi_i=1$ never enters the proof. Reversibility enters only through \cref{lem:setting_stationary_pow}, in \cref{lem:markov_subadd_right,lem:res_stationary}.

\subsection{Lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{stoch_pow}]\label{lem:stoch_pow}
If $A$ is stochastic, then $A^s$ is stochastic for every $s\in\N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $s$. The identity matrix is stochastic.

For the step, write $A^{s+1}=A^sA$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Its entries $\sum_k(A^s)_{ik}A_{kj}$ are sums of products of nonnegative numbers.
\item Its row sums are $\sum_k(A^s)_{ik}\sum_jA_{kj}=\sum_k(A^s)_{ik}=1$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{weighted_minkowski}]\label{lem:weighted_minkowski}
Let $\iota$ be a finite set and $c,f,g,F:\iota\to\R$ nonnegative with $F_i\le f_i+g_i$ for all $i$. Then
\[
\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_ic_iF_i^2}\le\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_ic_if_i^2}+\sqrt{\textstyle\sum_ic_ig_i^2}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply Cauchy--Schwarz to $u_i=\sqrt{c_i}f_i$ and $v_i=\sqrt{c_i}g_i$:
\[
\sum_ic_if_ig_i\le\sqrt{\textstyle\sum c_if_i^2\sum c_ig_i^2}.
\]
Since $0\le F_i\le f_i+g_i$,
\[
\sum_i c_iF_i^2\le\sum_ic_if_i^2+\sum_ic_ig_i^2+2\sum_ic_if_ig_i\le\Bigl(\sqrt{\textstyle\sum c_if_i^2}+\sqrt{\textstyle\sum c_ig_i^2}\Bigr)^2 .
\]
Both sides are nonnegative, so taking square roots gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{markov_subadd_expand}]\label{lem:markov_subadd_expand}
For arbitrary $\pi:[n]\to\R$, $A\in\R^{[n]\times[n]}$, $f:[n]\times[n]\to\R$ and $r,s\in\N$,
\[
\sum_{i,j}\pi_i(A^{r+s})_{ij}f_{ij}=\sum_{(i,k,j)\in[n]^3}\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}(A^s)_{kj}f_{ij}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Use $A^{r+s}=A^rA^s$, expand the matrix product, and reorder the finite triple sum.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{markov_subadd_left}]\label{lem:markov_subadd_left}
Let $A$ be stochastic, and let $\pi$, $f$, $r$, $s$ be arbitrary. Then
\[
\sum_{(i,k,j)}\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}(A^s)_{kj}f_{ik}=\sum_{i,k}\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}f_{ik}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write the triple sum as an iterated sum over $i,k,j$ and pull out the factors that do not depend on $j$. Then use $\sum_j(A^s)_{kj}=1$. This row-sum identity is proved by induction on $s$ exactly as in \cref{lem:stoch_pow}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{markov_subadd_right}]\label{lem:markov_subadd_right}
Let $A$ be stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$, and let $f$, $r$, $s$ be arbitrary. Then
\[
\sum_{(i,k,j)}\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}(A^s)_{kj}f_{kj}=\sum_{k,j}\pi_k(A^s)_{kj}f_{kj}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Rewrite the left side as
\[
\sum_k\Bigl(\sum_i\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_j(A^s)_{kj}f_{kj}\Bigr).
\]
By \cref{lem:setting_stationary_pow}, the first factor equals $\pi_k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_geom_sq_sqsum}]\label{lem:comp_geom_sq_sqsum}
If $0\le q<1$, the series $\sum_{s\ge0}s^2q^s$ converges to $q(1+q)/(1-q)^3$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The series converges by Mathlib's summability of $s^kq^s$; call its sum $T$. The $s=0$ term vanishes, so
\[
T=\sum_{s\ge0}(s+1)^2q^{s+1}.
\]
Expanding $(s+1)^2=s^2+2s+1$ and using $\sum sq^s=q/(1-q)^2$ and $\sum q^s=(1-q)^{-1}$ gives
\[
T=q\bigl(T+2q/(1-q)^2+(1-q)^{-1}\bigr).
\]
Solving this linear equation for $T$ gives $T(1-q)=q(1+q)/(1-q)^2$, which is the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{markov_subadd}]\label{lem:markov_subadd}
Assume the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\pi\ge0$;
\item $A$ is stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$;
\item $d:[n]\times[n]\to\R$ satisfies $d\ge0$ and $d_{ik}\le d_{ij}+d_{jk}$ for all $i,j,k$;
\item $D:\N\to\R$ satisfies $D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_i(A^s)_{ij}d_{ij}^2$ for all $s$.
\end{itemize}
Then $\sqrt{D(r+s)}\le\sqrt{D(r)}+\sqrt{D(s)}$ for all $r,s\in\N$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
On $[n]^3$ take the weights $c_{(i,k,j)}=\pi_i(A^r)_{ik}(A^s)_{kj}$. They are nonnegative by \cref{lem:stoch_pow}. With these weights:
\begin{itemize}
\item $D(r+s)=\sum c\,d_{ij}^2$ by \cref{lem:markov_subadd_expand};
\item $D(r)=\sum c\,d_{ik}^2$ by \cref{lem:markov_subadd_left};
\item $D(s)=\sum c\,d_{kj}^2$ by \cref{lem:markov_subadd_right}.
\end{itemize}
Apply \cref{lem:weighted_minkowski} with $F=d_{ij}$, $f=d_{ik}$, $g=d_{kj}$. The hypothesis $F\le f+g$ is the triangle inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_geom_mod_pow_le}]\label{lem:comp_geom_mod_pow_le}
For every integer $t>0$, $\bigl(t/(t+1)\bigr)^t\le 1/2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For $t=1$ the left side equals $1/2$.

For $t\ge2$, Bernoulli's inequality $(1+x)^t\ge1+tx$ with $x=1/t$ gives $(1+1/t)^t\ge2$. Since $t/(t+1)=(1+1/t)^{-1}$, the claim follows by inverting.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_geom_mod_hasSum}]\label{lem:comp_geom_mod_hasSum}
Let $t>0$, $0\le q<1$ and $f:\N\to\R$. The series $\sum_{s\ge0}q^sf(s\bmod t)$ converges to
\[
\frac{\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}q^rf(r)}{1-q^t}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For every $s$,
\[
\abs{q^sf(s\bmod t)}\le\Bigl(\sum_{r<t}\abs{f(r)}\Bigr)q^s .
\]
Hence the series $g(s)=q^sf(s\bmod t)$ is absolutely summable; let $\Sigma$ be its sum.

Since $g(s+t)=q^tg(s)$, the shifted series $\sum_sg(s+t)$ has sum $q^t\Sigma$. Splitting off the first $t$ terms gives
\[
\Sigma=\sum_{r<t}q^rf(r)+q^t\Sigma .
\]
Divide by $1-q^t\ne0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_block}]\label{lem:comp_block}
Let $t\in\N$ and $D:\N\to\R$ with $D\ge0$ and $\sqrt{D(r+s)}\le\sqrt{D(r)}+\sqrt{D(s)}$ for all $r,s$. Then for all $j,r\in\N$,
\[
D(jt+r)\le2j^2D(t)+2D(r).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Induction on $j$, using $(j+1)t+r=(jt+r)+t$, gives
\[
\sqrt{D(jt+r)}\le j\sqrt{D(t)}+\sqrt{D(r)}.
\]
Square both sides, which are nonnegative, and use $(a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_Dt}]\label{lem:comp_Dt}
Let $t>0$, and let $D:\N\to\R$ satisfy $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$ and the subadditivity of \cref{lem:comp_block}. Then
\[
D(t)\le4\cdot\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Squaring the subadditivity and using $2ab\le a^2+b^2$ gives $D(a+b)\le2D(a)+2D(b)$. For $0\le r<t$ this yields
\[
D(t)\le2D(r+1)+2D(t-1-r).
\]
Summing over $r<t$ and reflecting the second sum gives
\[
tD(t)\le2\sum_{r<t}D(r+1)+2\sum_{r<t}D(r).
\]
Now compare the two expressions for $\sum_{r\le t}D(r)$:
\[
\sum_{r<t}D(r+1)+D(0)=\sum_{r<t}D(r)+D(t).
\]
With $D(0)=0$ and $D(t)\ge0$ this gives $\sum_{r<t}D(r)\le\sum_{r<t}D(r+1)$. Hence $tD(t)\le4\sum_{s=1}^tD(s)$. Divide by $t$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_geom_sq}]\label{lem:comp_geom_sq}
Let $t>0$ and $q=t/(t+1)$. The series $\sum_sq^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2$ converges, and
\[
(1-q)\sum_sq^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le3 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Since $\lfloor s/t\rfloor\le s/t$,
\[
0\le q^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le t^{-2}s^2q^s .
\]
By \cref{lem:comp_geom_sq_sqsum}, this gives convergence and
\[
(1-q)\sum_sq^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2\le t^{-2}\frac{q(1+q)}{(1-q)^2}.
\]
With $1-q=1/(t+1)$ and $1+q=(2t+1)/(t+1)$, the right side equals $(2t+1)/t\le3$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_geom_mod}]\label{lem:comp_geom_mod}
Let $t>0$, $q=t/(t+1)$ and $f:\N\to\R$ with $f\ge0$. The series $\sum_sq^sf(s\bmod t)$ converges, and
\[
(1-q)\sum_sq^sf(s\bmod t)\le\frac2t\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}f(r).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $P=\sum_{r<t}q^rf(r)$ and $F=\sum_{r<t}f(r)$. Then $0\le P\le F$, because $0\le q^r\le1$.

By \cref{lem:comp_geom_mod_hasSum}, the series converges with sum $P/(1-q^t)$. By \cref{lem:comp_geom_mod_pow_le}, $1-q^t\ge1/2$, so the sum is at most $2P\le2F$.

Finally $(1-q)t=q\le1$, hence $(1-q)\cdot2F\le(2/t)F$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_real_range}]\label{lem:comp_real_range}
If $D:\N\to\R$ satisfies $D(0)=0$ and $D\ge0$, then for every $t\in\N$,
\[
\sum_{r=0}^{t-1}D(r)\le\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction, $\sum_{r=0}^{m}D(r)=D(0)+\sum_{s=1}^mD(s)$. With $m=t$ and $D(0)=0$,
\[
\sum_{r<t}D(r)+D(t)=\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
Now use $D(t)\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{comp_real}]\label{lem:comp_real}
Let $t>0$ and $q=t/(t+1)$. Let $D:\N\to\R$ satisfy $D(0)=0$, $D\ge0$ and $\sqrt{D(r+s)}\le\sqrt{D(r)}+\sqrt{D(s)}$ for all $r,s$. Then $\sum_sq^sD(s)$ converges and
\[
(1-q)\sum_sq^sD(s)\le28\cdot\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $s=\lfloor s/t\rfloor t+(s\bmod t)$. By \cref{lem:comp_block},
\[
q^sD(s)\le2D(t)\,q^s\lfloor s/t\rfloor^2+2q^sD(s\bmod t).
\]
The right side is summable by \cref{lem:comp_geom_sq,lem:comp_geom_mod}. The left side is nonnegative, so it is summable, and the sums compare.

Put $W=\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s)$. Multiply by $1-q\ge0$ and use $D(t)\ge0$:
\begin{align*}
(1-q)\sum_sq^sD(s)
&\le 6D(t)+2\cdot\frac2t\sum_{r<t}D(r)\\
&\le 6\cdot4W+4W=28W .
\end{align*}
The first step uses \cref{lem:comp_geom_sq,lem:comp_geom_mod}. The second uses \cref{lem:comp_Dt} and \cref{lem:comp_real_range}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_summable}]\label{lem:res_summable}
Let $A$ be stochastic, $0\le q<1$ and $i,j\in[n]$. The series $\sum_s(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$ converges.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By induction on $s$, the entries of $A^s$ are nonnegative and its rows sum to $1$, so $0\le(A^s)_{ij}\le1$. Hence the terms lie between $0$ and $(1-q)q^s$, whose series converges.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_comparison}]\label{lem:res_comparison}
Assume the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item $t>0$;
\item $\pi$ is a probability vector;
\item $A$ is stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$;
\item $x:[n]\to\ell_1$;
\item $q=t/(t+1)$;
\item $G\in\R^{[n]\times[n]}$ satisfies $G_{ij}=\sum_{s=0}^\infty(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$ for all $i,j$.
\end{itemize}
Then
\[
\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2\le28\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Put $D(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_i(A^s)_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$. We check the hypotheses of \cref{lem:comp_real}:
\begin{itemize}
\item $D(0)=0$, since $A^0=I$ and $\norm{x_i-x_i}=0$;
\item $D\ge0$, by $\pi\ge0$ and \cref{lem:stoch_pow};
\item subadditivity of $\sqrt D$ follows from \cref{lem:markov_subadd} with $d_{ij}=\norm{x_i-x_j}$, which satisfies the triangle inequality.
\end{itemize}

For each $i,j$, the series $\sum_s\pi_i(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$ converges to $\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$ by \cref{lem:res_summable}. Summing these finitely many series gives
\[
\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2=(1-q)\sum_sq^sD(s).
\]
Exchanging finite sums gives
\[
\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^tD(s)=\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
Now apply \cref{lem:comp_real}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_nonneg}]\label{lem:res_nonneg}
Let $A$ be stochastic, $0\le q<1$, and $G_{ij}=\sum_{s=0}^\infty(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$. Then $G_{ij}\ge0$ for all $i,j$.
\end{lemma}

\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_rowsum}]\label{lem:res_rowsum}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:res_nonneg}, $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$ for every $i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:res_summable}, the series $\sum_s\sum_j(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$ converges to $\sum_jG_{ij}$.

By \cref{lem:stoch_pow}, its terms equal $(1-q)q^s$. Their sum is $(1-q)(1-q)^{-1}=1$. Sums are unique.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_stationary_hasSum_fin}]\label{lem:res_stationary_hasSum_fin}
Let $f:[n]\times\N\to\R$ and $a:[n]\to\R$. If, for each $i$, the series $\sum_sf(i,s)$ converges to $a_i$, then $\sum_s\sum_if(i,s)$ converges to $\sum_ia_i$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_stationary}]\label{lem:res_stationary}
Let $\pi:[n]\to\R$ be arbitrary, $A$ stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$, $0\le q<1$, and $G$ as in \cref{lem:res_nonneg}. Then $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$ for every $j$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:res_summable,lem:res_stationary_hasSum_fin}, the series $\sum_s\sum_i\pi_i(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$ converges to $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}$.

By \cref{lem:setting_stationary_pow}, its terms equal $(1-q)q^s\pi_j$. Their sum is $\pi_j$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_left}]\label{lem:res_left}
Let $A$ be stochastic, $0\le q<1$, and $G$ as in \cref{lem:res_nonneg}. Then for all $i,j$,
\[
G_{ij}=(1-q)\delta_{ij}+q\sum_lA_{il}G_{lj}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Split off the $s=0$ term, which equals $(1-q)\delta_{ij}$. For the remaining terms use $(A^{s+1})_{ij}=\sum_lA_{il}(A^s)_{lj}$:
\[
\sum_s(1-q)q^{s+1}(A^{s+1})_{ij}=q\sum_s\sum_lA_{il}(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{lj}.
\]
By \cref{lem:res_summable}, the finite sum over $l$ and the series can be exchanged. This gives $q\sum_lA_{il}G_{lj}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{res_right}]\label{lem:res_right}
Under the same hypotheses, for all $i,j$,
\[
G_{ij}=(1-q)\delta_{ij}+q\sum_lG_{il}A_{lj}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
By \cref{lem:res_summable}, the series $\sum_s\sum_l(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{il}A_{lj}$ converges to $\sum_lG_{il}A_{lj}$.

Since $(A^{s+1})_{ij}=\sum_l(A^s)_{il}A_{lj}$, the shifted series $\sum_s(1-q)q^{s+1}(A^{s+1})_{ij}$ converges to $q\sum_lG_{il}A_{lj}$. Adding back the $s=0$ term $(1-q)\delta_{ij}$ gives the claim.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{flat_scalar}]\label{lem:flat_scalar}
Let $r,r'\in[0,1]$ and $d\in\{0,1\}$. With $\phi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$,
\[
\abs{\phi(r')-\phi(r)}\le6\abs{r-d}\abs{r'-r}+3(r'-r)^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
With $\delta=r'-r$ one has the polynomial identity
\[
\phi(r')-\phi(r)=\delta\bigl(6r(1-r)+\delta(3-4r-2r')\bigr).
\]
We bound the factors:
\begin{itemize}
\item $0\le6r(1-r)\le6\abs{r-d}$, since $r(1-r)\le r$ and $r(1-r)\le1-r$;
\item $\abs{3-4r-2r'}\le3$, since $r,r'\in[0,1]$.
\end{itemize}
Hence the second factor is at most $6\abs{r-d}+3\abs\delta$ in absolute value. Multiply by $\abs\delta$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{flat_increment}]\label{lem:flat_increment}
Assume the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\iota$ is a finite set and $w:\iota\to\R$ satisfies $w\ge0$;
\item $\phi:\R\to\R$ satisfies $\phi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$ for all $r$;
\item $e,u,u':\iota\to\R$ with $e_B\in\{0,1\}$ and $u_B,u'_B\in[0,1]$ for all $B$.
\end{itemize}
Then
\begin{align*}
\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(u'_B)-\phi(u_B)}\Bigr)^2
&\le72\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)^2\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B(u'_B-u_B)^2\Bigr)\\
&\quad+18\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B(u'_B-u_B)^2\Bigr)^2.
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Write $S$ for the sum on the left and set
\[
P=\sum w_B(u_B-e_B)^2,\quad Y=\sum w_B(u'_B-u_B)^2,\quad X=\sum w_B\abs{u_B-e_B}\abs{u'_B-u_B}.
\]
Summing \cref{lem:flat_scalar} with weights $w_B$ gives $0\le S\le6X+3Y$. Cauchy--Schwarz with $\sqrt{w_B}$ gives $X^2\le PY$. Hence
\[
S^2\le(6X+3Y)^2\le72X^2+18Y^2\le72PY+18Y^2 .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{flat_ineq}]\label{lem:flat_ineq}
Under the hypotheses of \cref{lem:flat_increment}, put
\[
F(v)=\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B(v_B-e_B)^2\Bigr)^2,\quad P=\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)^2,\quad L=\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)(u'_B-u_B).
\]
Then
\[
\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(u'_B)-\phi(u_B)}\Bigr)^2\le108\bigl(F(u')-F(u)-4PL\bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $Y=\sum w_B(u'_B-u_B)^2$. Expanding termwise gives
\[
\sum w_B(u'_B-e_B)^2=P+2L+Y .
\]
Hence
\[
R:=F(u')-F(u)-4PL=2PY+(2L+Y)^2 .
\]
Cauchy--Schwarz gives $L^2\le PY$. Therefore
\[
Y^2\le2(2L+Y)^2+8L^2\le2(2L+Y)^2+8PY .
\]
By \cref{lem:flat_increment},
\begin{align*}
S^2&\le72PY+18Y^2\\
&\le216PY+36(2L+Y)^2\\
&\le108R .
\end{align*}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{local_ineq_combine}]\label{lem:local_ineq_combine}
Let $m\in\N$, let $p,S_0,a,F_v,L_v\in\R$, and let $c,b,F_U,L:[m]\to\R$. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item $p\ge0$, $c\ge0$ and $p+\sum_jc_j=1$;
\item $pL_v+\sum_jc_jL_j=0$;
\item $a\le108(F_v^2-S_0^2-4S_0L_v)$;
\item $b_j\le108(F_{U,j}^2-S_0^2-4S_0L_j)$ for all $j$.
\end{itemize}
Then
\[
pa+\sum_jc_jb_j\le108\Bigl(pF_v^2+\sum_jc_jF_{U,j}^2-S_0^2\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Multiply the hypotheses by $p\ge0$ and $c_j\ge0$ and add them. Use $\sum c_j=1-p$ and $\sum c_jL_j=-pL_v$. The two terms $\mp432\,pS_0L_v$ cancel, and the coefficients of $S_0^2$ add up to $-108$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{local_ineq}]\label{lem:local_ineq}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $w\ge0$ and $\phi$ as in \cref{lem:flat_increment}. Let $e,u,v:\iota\to\R$, $U:[m]\to(\iota\to\R)$, $p\in\R$ and $c:[m]\to\R$. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item $p\ge0$, $c\ge0$ and $p+\sum_jc_j=1$;
\item $u_B=pv_B+\sum_jc_jU_{j,B}$ for all $B$;
\item $e_B\in\{0,1\}$ and $u_B,v_B,U_{j,B}\in[0,1]$ for all $j,B$.
\end{itemize}
Write $F(\cdot)$ as in \cref{lem:flat_ineq}. Then
\[
p\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(v_B)-\phi(u_B)}\Bigr)^2+\sum_jc_j\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(U_{j,B})-\phi(u_B)}\Bigr)^2
\le108\Bigl(pF(v)+\sum_jc_jF(U_j)-F(u)\Bigr).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
From the balance relation and $\sum c_j=1-p$,
\[
p(v_B-u_B)+\sum_jc_j(U_{j,B}-u_B)=0\qquad\text{for each }B .
\]
Multiply by $w_B(u_B-e_B)$ and sum over $B$. With $L_v=\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)(v_B-u_B)$ and $L_j=\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)(U_{j,B}-u_B)$ this gives $pL_v+\sum_jc_jL_j=0$.

Apply \cref{lem:flat_ineq} to the pair $(u,v)$ and to each pair $(u,U_j)$. Then conclude with \cref{lem:local_ineq_combine}, taking $S_0=\sum_Bw_B(u_B-e_B)^2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{global_sum}]\label{lem:global_sum}
Let $\pi:[n]\to\R$ with $\pi\ge0$, let $A,G\in\R^{[n]\times[n]}$ and $p,q\in\R$ with $p\ge0$. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G\ge0$ entrywise;
\item $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$ for all $j$;
\item $G_{kj}=p\delta_{kj}+q\sum_iG_{ki}A_{ij}$ for all $k,j$.
\end{itemize}
Let $J^d:[n]\to\R$ and $J^h,F^z,F^h:[n]\times[n]\to\R$ with $F^h\ge0$, and suppose that for all $k,i$
\begin{equation*}
pJ^d_i+q\sum_jA_{ij}J^h_{ij}\le108\Bigl(pF^z_{ki}+q\sum_jA_{ij}F^h_{kj}-F^h_{ki}\Bigr).
\end{equation*}
Then
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\Bigl(pJ^d_i+q\sum_jA_{ij}J^h_{ij}\Bigr)\le108\,p\sum_k\sum_i\pi_kG_{ki}F^z_{ki}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Fix $k$. Using the identity for $G$,
\[
\sum_iG_{ki}\Bigl(q\sum_jA_{ij}F^h_{kj}\Bigr)=\sum_j\Bigl(q\sum_iG_{ki}A_{ij}\Bigr)F^h_{kj}=\sum_jG_{kj}F^h_{kj}-pF^h_{kk}.
\]
Multiply the hypothesis for $(k,i)$ by $\pi_kG_{ki}\ge0$ and sum over $i$. The potential terms telescope by the display, so the right side becomes
\[
108\,\pi_k\Bigl(p\sum_iG_{ki}F^z_{ki}-pF^h_{kk}\Bigr)\le108\,p\sum_i\pi_kG_{ki}F^z_{ki},
\]
since $\pi_k,p,F^h_{kk}\ge0$.

Finally, by stationarity,
\[
\sum_i\pi_i(\cdots)_i=\sum_i\sum_k\pi_kG_{ki}(\cdots)_i .
\]
Exchange the two sums and sum the bounds over $k$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{h_props}]\label{lem:h_props}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $G,A\in\R^{[n]\times[n]}$ and $p,q\in\R$. Assume:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G\ge0$ and $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$ for all $i$;
\item $G_{ij}=p\delta_{ij}+q\sum_lA_{il}G_{lj}$ for all $i,j$;
\item $z:[n]\to(\iota\to\R)$ takes values in $[0,1]$;
\item $h_{iB}=\sum_jG_{ij}z_{jB}$ for all $i,B$.
\end{itemize}
Then $h_{iB}\in[0,1]$ and $h_{iB}=pz_{iB}+\sum_j(qA_{ij})h_{jB}$ for all $i,B$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
$h_{iB}$ is a convex combination of numbers in $[0,1]$, by the nonnegativity and row sums of $G$.

For the second identity, substitute the identity for $G_{ik}$ into $\sum_kG_{ik}z_{kB}$. This gives $pz_{iB}+\sum_kq\bigl(\sum_lA_{il}G_{lk}\bigr)z_{kB}$. Exchanging the finite sums gives $pz_{iB}+\sum_lqA_{il}h_{lB}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_coord_upper_shift}]\label{lem:cut_coord_upper_shift}
Let $a:[n]\to\R$ and $m<c$ be reals. Assume $a_i\ge m$ for all $i$, and $a_i<c\Rightarrow a_i=m$. Let $b':\Pow([n])\to\R$ satisfy:
\begin{itemize}
\item $b'\ge0$;
\item if $b'_B\ne0$, $j\in B$ and $\max(a_j,c)\le\max(a_i,c)$, then $i\in B$;
\item $\max(a_i,c)-\max(a_j,c)=\sum_Bb'_B(\one_B(i)-\one_B(j))$ for all $i,j$.
\end{itemize}
Then there is $b:\Pow([n])\to\R$ with:
\begin{itemize}
\item $b\ge0$;
\item if $b_B\ne0$, $j\in B$ and $a_j\le a_i$, then $i\in B$;
\item $a_i-a_j=\sum_Bb_B(\one_B(i)-\one_B(j))$ for all $i,j$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $B^*=\{i:c\le a_i\}$. For every $k$,
\[
a_k=\max(a_k,c)+(c-m)(\one_{B^*}(k)-1).
\]
Indeed, if $c\le a_k$ both sides equal $a_k$; otherwise $a_k=m$ and the right side is $c-(c-m)$.

Set $b_B=b'_B+(c-m)[B=B^*]$. Then $b\ge0$. The decomposition of $a_i-a_j$ follows by subtracting the identity for $j$ from that for $i$ and using the hypothesis on $b'$.

Upward closedness: suppose $b_B\ne0$, $j\in B$ and $a_j\le a_i$.
\begin{itemize}
\item If $B=B^*$, then $c\le a_j\le a_i$, so $i\in B^*$.
\item Otherwise $b'_B\ne0$ and $\max(a_j,c)\le\max(a_i,c)$, so the hypothesis gives $i\in B$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_coord_upper_reduce}]\label{lem:cut_coord_upper_reduce}
Let $a:[n]\to\R$ be non-constant, i.e.\ $a_i\ne a_j$ for some $i,j$. Then there are reals $m<c$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $a_i\ge m$ for all $i$;
\item $a_i<c\Rightarrow a_i=m$;
\item the set of values of $i\mapsto\max(a_i,c)$ has strictly smaller cardinality than the set of values of $a$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $V$ be the set of values of $a$, $m=\min V$, and $c=\min(V\setminus\{m\})$. The set $V\setminus\{m\}$ is nonempty because $a$ is non-constant. Then $m<c$, and any value below $c$ equals $m$.

The values of $\max(a,c)$ form exactly $V\setminus\{m\}$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\max(a_i,c)$ equals $c$ if $a_i\le c$, and equals $a_i>c>m$ otherwise; in both cases it lies in $V\setminus\{m\}$;
\item a value $a_i\ne m$ satisfies $a_i\ge c$, so $\max(a_i,c)=a_i$.
\end{itemize}
Removing $m\in V$ lowers the cardinality.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_coord_upper}]\label{lem:cut_coord_upper}
For every $a:[n]\to\R$ there is $b:\Pow([n])\to\R$ with the three properties in the conclusion of \cref{lem:cut_coord_upper_shift}.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
We prove by induction on $k$ that the claim holds for all $a$ taking at most $k$ values.

If $a$ is constant, take $b=0$. Otherwise \cref{lem:cut_coord_upper_reduce} gives $m<c$.
\begin{itemize}
\item For $k=0$, the cardinality inequality is impossible.
\item For $k+1$, the function $\max(a,c)$ takes at most $k$ values. The induction hypothesis gives $b'$ for it, and \cref{lem:cut_coord_upper_shift} produces $b$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_coord_core}]\label{lem:cut_coord_core}
For every $a:[n]\to\R$ there is $b:\Pow([n])\to\R$ with $b\ge0$ such that, for all $i,j$,
\[
a_i-a_j=\sum_Bb_B(\one_B(i)-\one_B(j)),\qquad \abs{a_i-a_j}=\sum_Bb_B\abs{\one_B(i)-\one_B(j)} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $b$ from \cref{lem:cut_coord_upper}. Suppose $a_j\le a_i$. For each $B$,
\[
b_B(\one_B(i)-\one_B(j))=b_B\abs{\one_B(i)-\one_B(j)} .
\]
This is trivial if $b_B=0$. If $b_B\ne0$ and $j\in B$, then $i\in B$ and both sides vanish. If $j\notin B$, the difference $\one_B(i)$ is nonnegative.

Hence $\abs{a_i-a_j}=a_i-a_j=\sum_Bb_B\abs{\cdots}$. The case $a_i\le a_j$ follows by symmetry.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_coord}]\label{lem:cut_coord}
For every $a:[n]\to\R$ there is $b:\Pow([n])\to\R$ satisfying:
\begin{itemize}
\item $b\ge0$;
\item $b_B\le2\sum_i\abs{a_i}$ for all $B$;
\item both identities of \cref{lem:cut_coord_core}.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $b$ from \cref{lem:cut_coord_core}. Replace $b_B$ by $0$ unless $B$ is nonempty and proper, i.e.\ unless some $i\in B$ and some $j\notin B$.

For the excluded $B$, $\one_B(i)-\one_B(j)=0$ for all $i,j$, so both identities persist.

For a proper nonempty $B$, pick $i\in B$ and $j\notin B$. The absolute identity gives
\[
b_B\le\abs{a_i-a_j}\le\abs{a_i}+\abs{a_j}\le2\sum\abs{a} .
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1_ext}]\label{lem:cut_l1_ext}
If $f,g\in\ell_1$ satisfy $f(k)=g(k)$ for all $k$, then $f=g$.
\end{lemma}

\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1_apply}]\label{lem:cut_l1_apply}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $x_0\in\ell_1$, $c:\iota\to\R$ and $\beta:\iota\to\ell_1$. For every $k$,
\[
\Bigl(x_0+\sum_Bc_B\beta_B\Bigr)(k)=x_0(k)+\sum_Bc_B\beta_B(k).
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{assembly_real_split}]\label{lem:assembly_real_split}
For arbitrary $\pi$, $A$, $p,q\in\R$, $a:[n]\to\R$ and $b:[n]\times[n]\to\R$,
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\Bigl(pa_i+q\sum_jA_{ij}b_{ij}\Bigr)=p\sum_i\pi_ia_i+q\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}b_{ij}.
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{assembly_real_finish}]\label{lem:assembly_real_finish}
Let $q,\tau,S_1,S_2,R\in\R$ with $q<1$ and $\tau(1-q)=q$. If $(1-q)S_1+qS_2\le108(1-q)R$, then $S_1+\tau S_2\le108R$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{assembly_real}]\label{lem:assembly_real}
Assume the following:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\pi\ge0$ and $A$ is stochastic;
\item $\iota$ is finite and $w:\iota\to\R$ satisfies $w\ge0$;
\item $z:[n]\to(\iota\to\R)$ with $z_{iB}\in\{0,1\}$;
\item $0\le q<1$ and $\tau(1-q)=q$;
\item $G\in\R^{[n]\times[n]}$ satisfies $G\ge0$, $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$, $\sum_i\pi_iG_{ij}=\pi_j$, and both identities of \cref{lem:res_left,lem:res_right}.
\end{itemize}
Write $\phi(r)=3r^2-2r^3$. Then there exists $h:[n]\to(\iota\to\R)$ with
\begin{align*}
&\sum_i\pi_i\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-\phi(h_{iB})}\Bigr)^2
+\tau\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(h_{iB})-\phi(h_{jB})}\Bigr)^2\\
&\qquad\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-z_{jB}}\Bigr)^2 .
\end{align*}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Let $h_{iB}=\sum_jG_{ij}z_{jB}$. By \cref{lem:h_props} with $p=1-q$, using the left identity, $h_{iB}\in[0,1]$ and
\[
h_{iB}=(1-q)z_{iB}+\sum_j(qA_{ij})h_{jB}.
\]
The weights $1-q$ and $qA_{ij}$ are nonnegative and sum to $1$ because $A$ is stochastic.

Fix $k,i$ and apply \cref{lem:local_ineq} with $e=z_k$, $u=h_i$, $v=z_i$, $U_j=h_j$, $p=1-q$ and $c_j=qA_{ij}$. For bits, $\phi(z_{iB})=z_{iB}$ and $(z_{iB}-z_{kB})^2=\abs{z_{kB}-z_{iB}}$. Hence the hypothesis of \cref{lem:global_sum} holds with
\begin{align*}
J^d_i&=\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-\phi(h_{iB})}\Bigr)^2, &
J^h_{ij}&=\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(h_{iB})-\phi(h_{jB})}\Bigr)^2,\\
F^z_{ki}&=\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{kB}-z_{iB}}\Bigr)^2, &
F^h_{ki}&=\Bigl(\sum_Bw_B(h_{iB}-z_{kB})^2\Bigr)^2\ge0 .
\end{align*}
\cref{lem:global_sum} applies with the right identity and stationarity. It gives
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\bigl((1-q)J^d_i+q\textstyle\sum_jA_{ij}J^h_{ij}\bigr)\le108(1-q)R,
\]
where $R$ is the double sum on the right of the claim. Split the left side by \cref{lem:assembly_real_split} and conclude with \cref{lem:assembly_real_finish}.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1_norm_combo}]\label{lem:cut_l1_norm_combo}
Let $\iota$ be finite, $f\in\ell_1$, $\beta:\iota\to\ell_1$ and $d:\iota\to\R$. Suppose $\beta_B(k)\ge0$ for all $B,k$ and $\abs{f(k)}=\sum_B\beta_B(k)d_B$ for all $k$. Then
\[
\norm f=\sum_B\norm{\beta_B}d_B .
\]
\end{lemma}

\PY{+w}{      }\PY{n}{rw}\PY{+w}{ }\PY{o}{[}\PY{n}{hnorm\PYZus{}β}\PY{+w}{ }\PY{n}{B}\PY{o}{]}
\end{Verbatim}
\end{leanblock}
\begin{proof}
We have $\norm f=\sum_k\abs{f(k)}=\sum_k\sum_B\beta_B(k)d_B$. Each series $\sum_k\beta_B(k)$ converges, because $\beta_B\in\ell_1$. Hence the finite sum and the series can be exchanged, giving $\sum_Bd_B\sum_k\beta_B(k)$. Finally $\sum_k\beta_B(k)=\sum_k\abs{\beta_B(k)}=\norm{\beta_B}$, since $\beta_B\ge0$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1_vectors_summable_fsum}]\label{lem:cut_l1_vectors_summable_fsum}
Let $f:\iota\to(\N\to\R)$ with each $f_i$ summable, and let $s\subseteq\iota$ be finite. Then $k\mapsto\sum_{i\in s}f_i(k)$ is summable.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1_vectors}]\label{lem:cut_l1_vectors}
For every $n$ and $x:[n]\to\ell_1$ there is $\beta:\Pow([n])\to\ell_1$ such that $\beta_B(k)\ge0$ for all $B,k$, and for all $i,j,k$:
\[
x_i(k)=x_j(k)+\sum_B(\one_B(i)-\one_B(j))\beta_B(k),\qquad
\abs{(x_i-x_j)(k)}=\sum_B\beta_B(k)\abs{\one_B(i)-\one_B(j)} .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
For each coordinate $k$, apply \cref{lem:cut_coord} to $a=(x_i(k))_i$ and choose the resulting $b^{(k)}$. Put $\beta_B(k)=b^{(k)}_B$.

Then $0\le\beta_B(k)\le2\sum_i\abs{x_i(k)}$. The right side is summable in $k$ by \cref{lem:cut_l1_vectors_summable_fsum}, since each $x_i\in\ell_1$. Hence $\beta_B\in\ell_1$.

The two identities are those of \cref{lem:cut_coord} at coordinate $k$, using $(x_i-x_j)(k)=x_i(k)-x_j(k)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{cut_l1}]\label{lem:cut_l1}
Let $n>0$ and $x:[n]\to\ell_1$. Then there exist $w:\Pow([n])\to\R$, $z:[n]\to(\Pow([n])\to\R)$ and $T:\R^{\Pow([n])}\to\ell_1$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
\item $w\ge0$ and $z_{iB}\in\{0,1\}$;
\item $T(z_i)=x_i$;
\item $\norm{T(u)-T(u')}\le\sum_Bw_B\abs{u_B-u'_B}$ for all $u,u'$;
\item $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-z_{jB}}$ for all $i,j$.
\end{itemize}
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $\beta$ from \cref{lem:cut_l1_vectors} and let $i_0$ be the first index (it exists because $n>0$). Set
\[
w_B=\norm{\beta_B},\qquad z_{iB}=\one_B(i),\qquad T(u)=x_{i_0}+\sum_B(u_B-z_{i_0B})\beta_B .
\]
We check the properties in turn.
\begin{itemize}
\item $T(z_i)=x_i$: compare coordinates, using \cref{lem:cut_l1_apply}, the signed identity with $j=i_0$, and \cref{lem:cut_l1_ext}.
\item Contraction: $T(u)-T(u')=\sum_B(u_B-u'_B)\beta_B$, and the triangle inequality bounds its norm by $\sum_B\abs{u_B-u'_B}\norm{\beta_B}$.
\item Distance identity: \cref{lem:cut_l1_norm_combo} with $f=x_i-x_j$ and $d_B=\abs{z_{iB}-z_{jB}}$.
\end{itemize}
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[\leanname{assembly}]\label{lem:assembly}
Assume the hypotheses of \cref{lem:assembly_real} on $\pi$, $A$, $w$, $z$, $q$, $\tau$ and $G$. Assume moreover that $x:[n]\to\ell_1$ and $T:\R^\iota\to\ell_1$ satisfy:
\begin{itemize}
\item $T(z_i)=x_i$;
\item $\norm{T(u)-T(u')}\le\sum_Bw_B\abs{u_B-u'_B}$;
\item $\norm{x_i-x_j}=\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-z_{jB}}$.
\end{itemize}
Then there is $y:[n]\to\ell_1$ with
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+\tau\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Take $h$ from \cref{lem:assembly_real} and set $y_i=T(\phi(h_i))$, where $\phi$ acts coordinatewise.

By the contraction property and $T(z_i)=x_i$:
\begin{itemize}
\item $\norm{x_i-y_i}\le\sum_Bw_B\abs{z_{iB}-\phi(h_{iB})}$;
\item $\norm{y_i-y_j}\le\sum_Bw_B\abs{\phi(h_{iB})-\phi(h_{jB})}$.
\end{itemize}
Square these bounds and multiply by the nonnegative weights $\pi_i$ and $\pi_iA_{ij}$. Also $\tau\ge0$, since $\tau(1-q)=q\ge0$ and $1-q>0$.

Summing, the left side is bounded by the left side of \cref{lem:assembly_real}. The right side of that lemma equals $108\sum\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2$ by the distance identity.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Let $n,t>0$, $\pi$, $A$ and $x$ be as in the target statement.

\emph{Cut decomposition.} \cref{lem:cut_l1} gives $w$, $z$ and $T$ with $\iota=\Pow([n])$.

\emph{Parameters.} Put $q=t/(t+1)$. Then $0\le q<1$ and $q(t+1)=t$, so $\tau=t$ satisfies $\tau(1-q)=q$.

\emph{Resolvent.} Define $G_{ij}=\sum_{s=0}^\infty(1-q)q^s(A^s)_{ij}$. By \cref{lem:res_nonneg,lem:res_rowsum,lem:res_stationary,lem:res_left,lem:res_right}:
\begin{itemize}
\item $G\ge0$ and $\sum_jG_{ij}=1$;
\item $\pi G=\pi$, which uses reversibility through \cref{lem:setting_stationary_pow};
\item $G$ satisfies both resolvent identities.
\end{itemize}

\emph{Construction.} \cref{lem:assembly}, with $\pi\ge0$ and these data, yields $y:[n]\to\ell_1$ with
\[
\sum_i\pi_i\norm{x_i-y_i}^2+t\sum_{i,j}\pi_iA_{ij}\norm{y_i-y_j}^2\le108\sum_{i,j}\pi_iG_{ij}\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]

\emph{Comparison.} \cref{lem:res_comparison} bounds the right side by
\[
108\cdot28\sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\frac1t\sum_{s=1}^t(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\norm{x_i-x_j}^2 .
\]
Since $108\cdot28=3024$, this is the asserted inequality.
\end{proof}

\section{Independent review}

A referee model (claude-opus-5-5), which took no part in the formalization or the proof, compared the verified Lean file with the source. Verdict: \textbf{FAITHFUL}.

\paragraph{Definitions.} \leanname{L1Space} is \leanname{lp} of $\mathbb N \to \mathbb R$ with exponent $1$. Its norm is $\sum_k |x(k)|$, so this is the real Banach space $\ell_1$. It is indexed from $0$ rather than $1$, which is immaterial.

\leanname{IsProbVec} requires nonnegative entries summing to one. Zero entries are allowed, as in the source.

\leanname{IsStochasticMatrix} requires nonnegative entries and every row sum equal to $1$.

\leanname{IsReversibleWrt} is detailed balance: $\pi_i a_{ij} = \pi_j a_{ji}$ for all $i,j$.

All four definitions match the source exactly. The auxiliary \leanname{setting_consistent} exhibits an instance satisfying all three predicates, so the hypotheses are not vacuous.

\paragraph{Statement.} Quantification is over the source's objects:
\begin{itemize}
\item $n,t$ positive naturals;
\item $\pi$ a probability vector on $\mathrm{Fin}\,n$;
\item $A$ stochastic and reversible with respect to $\pi$;
\item $x : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \ell_1$.
\end{itemize}
The hypothesis $0<n$ is automatic anyway, since a probability vector on an empty index set cannot exist.

The conclusion asserts the existence of $y : \mathrm{Fin}\,n \to \ell_1$ satisfying
\[
\sum_i \pi_i \|x_i-y_i\|^2 + t\sum_{i,j}\pi_i a_{ij}\|y_i-y_j\|^2 \le 3024 \sum_{i,j}\pi_i\Bigl(\tfrac1t\sum_{s\in[1,t]}(A^s)_{ij}\Bigr)\|x_i-x_j\|^2 .
\]
This is the source inequality verbatim. In particular, $A^s$ is the matrix power, the Ces\`aro average runs over $s=1,\dots,t$, and the constant is $3024$.

No extra hypotheses are present, and nothing the source proves is assumed. The statement is not trivially satisfiable: for example, $y = x$ does not in general make the left side small relative to the right.

\paragraph{Proof.} The formal proof follows the source's architecture, with the probabilistic parts replaced by deterministic matrix identities.

\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Cuts.} \leanname{cut_coord_upper}, \leanname{cut_coord_core}, \leanname{cut_coord}, \leanname{cut_l1_vectors} and \leanname{cut_l1} carry out Lemma 1.
\begin{itemize}
\item They build, coordinatewise, nonnegative cut weights indexed by all subsets of $\mathrm{Fin}\,n$, with nested-cut sign control.
\item The bound $b_B(k)\le 2\sum_i|x_i(k)|$ gives membership in $\ell_1$.
\item The affine map $T(u)=x_{i_0}+\sum_B (u_B - \mathbf 1_{i_0\in B})\beta_B$ is shown to satisfy $T(z_i)=x_i$, contractivity, and $\|x_i-x_j\|=\sum_B w_B|z_i(B)-z_j(B)|$.
\item Zero weights are allowed, so the ``all points coincide'' case needs no separate treatment.
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Flat map.} \leanname{flat_scalar}, \leanname{flat_increment} and \leanname{flat_ineq} prove Lemma 2 with the constant $108$. They use the same scalar bound $6|a||\delta|+3\delta^2$ and Cauchy--Schwarz.

\item \textbf{Martingale step.} The source's Corollary 3 and the stopped-walk martingale are replaced by a deterministic argument.
\begin{itemize}
\item \leanname{res_left} and \leanname{res_right} establish the resolvent identities $G = pI + qAG = pI + qGA$ for $G=\sum_s p q^s A^s$.
\item \leanname{h_props} establishes the harmonic identity (2) for $h=Gz$.
\item \leanname{local_ineq} is the one-step conditional-expectation version of Lemma 2: the linear term cancels by the balance relation.
\item \leanname{global_sum} sums these local inequalities with weights $\pi_k G_{ki}$. The right resolvent identity then telescopes the potentials, and the initial nonnegative potential is discarded.
\end{itemize}
This yields $B + tE_A \le 108\sum_{i,j}\pi_i G_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|^2$ (\leanname{assembly_real}, \leanname{assembly}). This is exactly the bound the source obtains from (stopped-bound) and (jump-identity). It is a legitimate deterministic rendering of the expectation computation.

\item \textbf{Comparison.} \leanname{markov_subadd}, \leanname{comp_block}, \leanname{comp_Dt}, \leanname{comp_geom_sq}, \leanname{comp_geom_mod}, \leanname{comp_real} and \leanname{res_comparison} prove Lemma 4 with constant $28$, phrased directly in terms of $D(s)=\sum\pi_i (A^s)_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|^2$.
\begin{itemize}
\item Subadditivity of $\sqrt{D}$ uses stationarity of $\pi$ under $A^r$, derived from reversibility.
\item The bound $\mathbb E J^2 \le 3$ and the bound $\mathbb P(R=r) \le 2/t$ are proved via explicit series.
\end{itemize}

\item \textbf{Assembly.} The final \leanname{linarith} combines the two bounds: $108\cdot 28 = 3024$.
\end{itemize}

No lemma is weaker than the step it represents, and no step is assumed rather than proved.

\paragraph{Concerns.} None
